sources.title: M.H.Kalavathy, Ethnical and Socio-Cultural Background of Marine Fishing Communities in Orissa, in U.Tietze (ed.), Artisanal Marine Fisherfolk of Orissa
sources.publication: Vidyapuri, Cuttack, December1985; BOBP/MIS/3, FAO-hosted scan
sources.status: Actual original PDFs inspected in preceding Kaibarta research and reused here, including chapter3 beginning and southern-coast material
sources.locator: Chapter3 printed59–61 (PDF1–3), introduction printed5–6; frontmatterPDF4 imprint
claims: In the study's southern Odisha context, Noliyas is a local designation covering Jalari and Vodabalija fishing groups of Telugu origin. Treat this as source-specific naming, not one universal alias or identity rule.

The author describes Jalari settlements concentrated in Ganjam and Vodabalija settlements extending towards Puri and southern Cuttack. Movement is described over preceding decades, not one founding migration.
The account distinguishes fishing, marketing and processing work and describes locally organised councils. Such descriptions belong to1985research, not unchanging rules for descendants.
limits: Tamil word antiquity and very early fishing dates depend on earlier literature not independently read; omit as proven origin.
Study sampled248households across10villages; only4southern villages, one Jalari and3Vodabalija. Do not call every southern fisher Nolia.
Do not transfer Kaibarta-specific claims from northern section.

sources.title: Priya Gupta, Survival and Resilience of Two Village Communities in Coastal Orissa: A Comparison of Coping with Disasters
sources.locator: Printed2(PDF4) site description; printed15–16(PDF17–18) Ethnicity, Local Leadership and Networks; printed8(PDF10) place attachment
claims: The study compares a predominantly Noliya fishing village in Chatrapur block,Ganjam, with a nearby agricultural village. Its findings are local, not an Odisha-wide community survey.
The fishing families spoke Telugu and had lived there long enough that they did not know when their group first settled. Many also spoke Odia; younger members studied through Odia and English.

Gupta records a strong sense of being part of Odisha rather than Andhra Pradesh despite the language difference. She links local community identity to shared occupation and relationships, not merely language.
Her account also describes attachment to the sea and village. This is a lived-history example, not proof of ancient ancestry or a universal attitude to relocation.
limits: Working paper explicitly presents work in progress.
Exact fieldworkdates not found; say published2010, not conducted2010.
Village is not named in inspected site description; do not identify it by matching householdcounts.
Do not reproduce blanket legal-status assertions or caste-rank statements in the surrounding discussion.
Educational and livelihood descriptions are period observations, not current facts.

sources.title: Vineetha Venugopal, Biswa Swaroop Das, Naveen Namboothri and Aarthi Sridhar, Commoning Coastal Odisha
sources.status: Actual original institutional research PDF inspected
sources.locator: Printed13 methods;17 settlement profile;18–19 institutions;20 shared landing;22 jetty house;24 shared spaces and jetty disagreement
claims: Scoping began June2019 and included Sana Nolia Nuagaon among selected Ganjam settlements, using interviews, group discussions and walks. Detailed participatory mapping focused on Purnabandha, not the whole Nolia community.
The report identifies Nolia Nuagaon as a Telugu marine-fishing settlement divided into Bada and Sana sections.
It documents Nolia Nuagaon fishers sharing Purnabandha shore spaces; women from both settlements used the jetty building to dry fish when it was not serving fishing operations.

Fishing committees presented grievances and sought compensation for damaged gear; the seven-village Maa Ganga Devi Fishing Society included Nolia Nuagaon and resolved inter-village fishing disputes. These are dated observations of institutions, not current legal guarantees.
limits: Do not treat every Telugu village in the report as one caste.
Do not infer caste from settlementname alone; combine clearly scoped earlier naming evidence.
Shared spaces also generated disagreements; avoid romanticising unanimous harmony.
Do not repeat contemporary accessrights or conservationrule claims without separate current verification.

claims: The district account describes migration from the south, particularly Andhra and Tamil Nadu, and names Jalarulu and Oda Baliji groups with Telugu as mother tongue. It supplies no single dated migration event.
It attributes a Jalandhara descent claim to the Jalarulu group. This is an origin tradition, not evidence of actual descent or when a caste formed.
It describes Dola Purnima worship associated with Narasingha Swamy and Simhachalam, citing the1961Nuagolabandh monograph. If used, explicitly identify this as an older reported local practice.
limits: Much undated present-tense custom description likely reproduces older sources; not evidence of today's uniform practices.
Avoid innatecharacter/physique claims and reductive clothing, poverty or rank generalisations.
Optional source; three stronger originals already support substantive narrative.

recommended_narrative: Question: how do Telugu-speaking coastal communities belong to Odisha, and what do settlement histories and shore work reveal beyond a simple caste label?
Begin with scoped1985name usage and distinguish Jalari/Vodabalija rather than forcing one genealogy.
Describe movement along coast without a single invented arrivaldate; use2010fieldtestimony to explain why earliestsettlement remains unresolved.
Use Gupta's language and belonging observation as concrete heritage insight: Telugu, Odia education and attachment toOdisha can coexist.
Show shore as a shared workplace through2019–2021Nolia Nuagaon/Purnabandha examples, including women's dryingwork and local institutions.
Optional brief attributedJalandhara tradition or historicalDola practice if necessary, but noquota and no genericritual catalogue.
Close with openfamilyhistory/trainingquestions; inheritedoccupation is not compulsory for descendants.
